utterances.text: Okay. That's what I meant by a team but any other building, empty building, which needed security at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly it must have been something important. That's why we were sent out there to provide security. After all, our leading people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long were your duty shifts while you were engaged as a member of the 2nd Company of the PJP in Srebrenica town in the period of 12 through 20 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all depended on the service roster. Sometimes 12 hours, sometimes 24 hours, but at any rate, we had these buildings there where we could get some rest, get some sleep, some people would be on duty, others would be sleeping and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During this time period when you were in Srebrenica town as a member of the 2nd Company of the PJP, did you personally have the ability to remain in contact with the PJP -- the other PJP from the 2nd, 1st, or 6th Company by any means, you personally?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no contact and I did not have the possibility of having any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would that -- strike that. A little bit different question: Did you have the means to have any contact with anyone outside of Srebrenica town during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not. I personally had no means of contacting anyone outside the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for your questions. I thank you the interpreters for the extra five minutes and Your Honours I've completed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey, it was a bit uncertain to me whether you would not be available after the break or because -- I have a few questions as well. I don't know whether you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can stay, Mr. President, if need be and I did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It sounded rather urgent that you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it is, but this is of course my priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try then to be as brief as possible and continue for another couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I just had one question on one point Mr. Ivetic just made if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I put my question first, then you may consider whether you still have only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, when you were at the Srebrenica police station, did you ever look at this what is called the log-book which started on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took a look at that. I had the opportunity of seeing that book, the book was in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was the purpose of the book, to record what assignments were given or to record who had been where?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This book was used for assignments, assignments for individual policemen, to see who was where, carrying out which duty. That is to say all policemen could take a look at that and see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if you say assignments for individual policemen to see who was where, rather you'd say to see who had to go where to carry out what duty? Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether someone went there is not recorded here?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not recorded here, but this person would have to go or otherwise face certain sanctions or other disciplinary methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it may well be that he went ill or that there was a casualty in his family and that he finally didn't go without being punished or disciplined?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. That could have happened too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we do not know what actually happened but we know what tasks were assigned. Now, until when did this log-book, as it was called, function?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a temporary book. That is to say momentarily, while we were up there, so that people would know where we were being sent and where we were carrying out our duties. Later on when all of that was over I went home to get some rest and then I would return to Srebrenica. That is to say after the 20th I went to get some rest, and then other books were set up and other records in relation to the police station of Srebrenica and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You said other books were set up. When was that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These other books were started after the 20th, when this 2nd Company finished these duties in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, until when does this log-book last? I don't know whether it's still in front of you. But otherwise, if it's still there -- the original. Could we have it? Could we have a look at it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, looking at the log-book, the last entry is the 3rd of August and you said that new logbooks were started at the -- once you had returned, I think you said after the 20th. Why does it go on until 39rd of August? What happened on the 3rd of August that it was suddenly interrupted although not yet full?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity of looking through that entire book, but I know that it was kept until that period. I went after that to get some rest at home in Bratunac and probably it went on, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any -- I'm also looking at the Prosecution, are there any follow-up books known? Or is this what we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is what we have. We -- I can give you information on when and where we got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there is no follow-up version of the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not that we have. There may have been one, as you might imagine. I can - I think the investigator that did it is still with us so I can check, but as you can imagine we only took the ones we thought were relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the sequence of these kind of log-books may be relevant as well. That's -- of course if you have any further news on that, then you'll certainly put it to the -- I have no further questions for you. You have no explanation why it all stopped on the 3rd of August suddenly, in the middle of a book which was far from full?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I did not keep records in this book. I did not have any activities. The only thing I did was to start this record and to write that on the front page. I don't know what was written in there afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the reason that you were the one who had to write on the cover?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably because I was the first one to be in that station, and I had worked there before the war, and I was probably the first of those people who had worked there before the war to come, and that's why I did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I see, and that's not part of the excerpt and the parties are invited to upload that as well, that on the first page after the cover, you didn't fill that in, so you -- or did you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it from here in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can also I think look up 65 ter number 30998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that helps us then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it may -- that's the Prosecution's upload of the same book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then it should be page 2 or 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, for completeness, and I believe this has been scanned and should be in e-court, but these two original documents were also in the book when found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what are they or could we have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's just a list of things and some sort -- a list of people, excuse me, and receipt of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you meanwhile take care that we have on the screen the 65 ter number Mr. Ivetic was so kind to give?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think Your Honours wanted page 2 of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it -- let me just.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can upload the entire -- the entire one under our number if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I just want to have a look at it. If you look at your page service roster log-book, so you were asked to write on the outside but then you gave it to someone else to write on the first page what is this about?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody else did it. This is not my handwriting. Somebody else wrote this. It wasn't me. The service roster log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- okay. I leave it to that at this moment. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey, but of course we have no idea what it all is. I take it that it lacks such relevance that you haven't drawn our attention to it in any other way. I give it -- I return it to Madam Registrar. I have no further questions. And the log-book may be returned to the -- Madam Registrar, the log-book can be returned to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last document on the issue raised by Mr. Ivetic about his lack of ability to communicate in Srebrenica. If we could have 65 ter 4052 on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sure you knew a man that was born in Bratunac named Zeljko Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Ninkovic was not born in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you know him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see from this document from Dragomir Vasic, that it was known to the CSB the same day that he was killed in the combat on Konjevic Polje. Surely you would have gotten the word that this Bratunac member of the 1st PJP was killed within a day or a few days after this tragic death?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me? Are you -- I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Surely you heard within a few days of his death?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about his death, but I personally did not contact anyone. In fact I was unable to contact anyone. Our superiors probably were able to get in touch with somebody, but I personally could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4052 receives number P6688, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. No further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On this log-book that may be helpful for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you present or did you -- excuse me -- let -- did you know that the Office of the Prosecutor on 2nd of June, 2002, went to the MUP Bratunac Public Security Service building and seized the original of the Srebrenica log-book, 585 in this case?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when I earlier said when you were asked whether you knew Mr. Zeljko Ninkovic, when you said that he was not born in Bratunac, I was too early because Mr. McCloskey had made that part of his question. So you are fully right in telling us first of all that you do not know him to have been born in Bratunac. Apologies for that. Any further questions, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your evidence, Mr. Deronjic. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, Mr. Ivetic, the witness said -- to give any follow-up to his remark that he was unfairly treated. Is the Defence of the same view that we don't have to pay further attention to it or would you like us to review the interview and then verify whether there is any -- whether the witness's claim is reliable or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have no problem with you looking at the interview. In fact I think I had subsequent to that asked for the whole interview to be reviewed to verify that the only document that was discussed as having been reviewed at that time was the Bratunac log-book, not the Srebrenica log-book, as had had been implied by Mr. McCloskey's line of questions. It's uploaded into the system, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Ivetic, I asked you whether you -- you wanted us to follow up. The Chamber itself, having heard what the witness said, is not inclined to initiate any follow-up unless one of the parties -- and I would say if the witness had been exaggerating then it might be -- if the witness has not exaggerated, then I can imagine that the Defence would have an interest in the Chamber further looking at --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why I said we would like to have the Chamber -- I guess you can't look at it, you can listen to the audio, it's my understanding it's only an audio recording, the transcript of which I think the Prosecution may have uploaded I don't have a number for it but do I have a copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then I take it that you will identify the portions where you consider that there was some merit in what the witness said about being unfairly treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then I would have to listen to it I only have had access to the transcript at this time, Your Honours. So I have been working off the English transcript of that interview. I have not had the audio to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether the Defence had had any specific interest in that, and if you say you should listen to the audio for us apparently to find out where perhaps a voice was raised or not, without you yourself having listened to it, that is not the way in which this Chamber works.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if there is any concern about the way in which the witness was treated, please identify it and we will carefully verify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will then take that under advisement and I will petition the Court if we decide, we can find those sections to clearly point you in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Well, we went quite a bit beyond the time we had on our minds. We take a break and we will resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, a few matters. First of all, in relation to witness Nikolic, the parties have been granted access now to the e-mail exchange. If there is any intention to give it any follow-up then the Chamber would like to hear that as quickly as possible because otherwise we would instruct VWS to inform the witness that he's not in any way limited any more in his communication with other persons about his role as a witness. So therefore, in order not to let him wait, Mr. Ivetic, I saw there was even a quick consultation, no follow-up from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From the Defence side, no follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just verifying right now if I could report back later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could do that so that the witness should not wait too long. Then there is another matter. There is a pending motion on -- well it's not a motion. It's an objection to the testimony of Mr. Pejic. And the Chamber would like to decide on that objection and do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you want to hear our -- I think we have some additional submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you would know that as matters stand now, that the Chamber was about to deny the objection, would that mean that you would still want to strengthen your case? Which sometimes makes sense. I'm not kidding, but if it's just about the outcome, then you shouldn't be too concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then probably we will have to deal with that some other time. But if it's -- I don't want to spoil your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you're not spoiling the decision in any way, Mr. Lukic. Then I give the decision. I'll not limit myself to that. But first the decision. In the 10th of June, 2014, response to the Defence Rule 92 ter motion for Milan Pejic, the Prosecution objected to the admission of paragraphs 19 to 23 of Pejic's statement on the basis that they contain tu quoque evidence. On the 4th of July the Defence filed a revised statement; however, paragraphs 19 to 23 have not changed significantly and the Chamber considers the Prosecution's objections to apply mutatis mutandis to the new statement. On the 16th of July, 2014, the Defence filed an additional submission, arguing that paragraphs 19 to 23 of the statement are relevant and that the Prosecution's objections are without merit and should be dismissed. The Chamber notes the Prosecution's recent filing of the 18th of July on this matter and hereby grants the Prosecution leave to surreply. Generally, the Chamber does not consider evidence to be tu quoque solely on the basis of its subject matter. In this case, the Defence argues that paragraphs 19 to 23 provide evidence that, and I quote, "There was incoming fire from ABiH heavy weapons" which it submits caused a threat to the Serb population of Sarajevo. It argues that as a result, there was, and I quote again, "A legitimate justification for VRS military actions against the ABiH in and around Sarajevo, as well as for VRS heavy weapons fire." Lastly, the Defence submits the proposed evidence is relevant to the placement of these ABiH weapons in relation to the VRS as well as the manner in which they were produced. In its surreply, the Prosecution argues that the assertions made by the Defence in relation to Prosecution witnesses are unsubstantiated, that the Defence misconstrues the Prosecution's position as well as the Defence and in doing so creates a justification for admitting otherwise inadmissible tu quoque evidence. In sum, the Prosecution submits that the Defence fails to present a legally valid reason for the admission of Pejic's evidence. The Chamber understands the Defence to argue that paragraphs 19 to 23 of the witness's statement relates to motive for VRS military action in Sarajevo during the relevant period in the indictment, which, and in this respect the Chamber finds that the statement is not deprived of relevance or probative value however limited it may be, and for that reason, the Chamber denies the Prosecution's objections focusing exclusively on tu quoque and permit the tendering of Pejic's statement inclusive of paragraphs 19 to 23. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the matter. Now, having concluded the decision, this does not mean that the Chamber does not have major concerns about this type of statements and the way in which time and also court time is used, but it will address that in its more general guidance, which is to follow later this week. But the tu quoque objection is denied. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would call Mr. Pejic, Milan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And just to inform Your Honours and Ms. Stewart, I didn't have time to ask her kindly our intention is to play video marked as D523 MFI'd. D523. Of course, asking her assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pejic. Before you give evidence, the rules require you to make a solemn declaration. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to you, too. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pejic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, you will first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just ask the assistance of the usher to provide the witness with a clean statement, of course, to show it to the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. Lukic referred to D523, that's a Defence exhibit. That's a video. Ms. Stewart informs me she was not informed about this video in advance. The CD sits at her desk and is not in Sanction, so she is unable to play that video for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will try to sort it out differently. I think my colleague Mr. Ivetic will leave now and try to see if he can do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's an important task to fulfil, Mr. Lukic please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Pejic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have in front of you a written statement and now I would like this statement to be -- or rather 1D1622 to be placed on the screen in front of you. Doctor, do you see this statement in front of you and you also have it in hard copy? For administrative reasons I will now ask you whether you have had an opportunity to look at the statement before.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The signature that we see here on the screen, on the first page, whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the last page. The signature on the last page, whose is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: This is also my signature and this was signed on the 29th of May, 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This statement that you have in front of you, does it reflect accurately what you told the Defence team representing General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I think it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this statement into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1622 receives number D589, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D589 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honours, I would have -- first read a short summary and then have a few questions for this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Witness worked as a doctor in Kosevo clinic as of from 1979, specialised in the diseases of the ear, throat, and nose. As of May 1992, witness worked in the military hospital in Blazuj. Witness will testify on overall situation in Sarajevo before and after conflict emerged. He will explain circumstances of creation of this hospital in Blazuj. Since he worked in Kosevo Hospital for a longer period, he will confirm the situation worsened in April 1992, where patients of Kosevo Hospital feared for own security while heading to Kosevo Hospital, and they avoid arriving for treatment. He will explain his knowledge on existence of paramilitaries in Sarajevo at the beginning of the conflict. In April 1992, attack occurred on hotel in Ilidza, where UNPROFOR members were located. Many people were wounded and killed. He had to give to those people first medical aid, since it was not possible to leave for Sarajevo. He will testify on creation of Crisis Staff in the hospital and its activity. He will explain circumstances of organisation and work of hospital in Blazuj, on records kept, on number and ethnicity of patients, on medical care in this hospital in relevant period. He will also testify on their injuries and type of weapons which caused those injuries. He will also explain security situation in and around the hospital, during the period of conflict. The witness will also testify on attack from October of 1992 where bus station in Ilidza was shelled, where many civilians were killed and wounded. And our plan is to show this witness the video we just mentioned minutes ago, and to ask for his knowledge on that video and smuggling on military equipment in -- in the medical -- actually oxygen bottles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you want to ask that, that sounds -- we've heard that now a couple of times now. Is this witness in a position to add something substantial to what we have heard already? As you know, the Chamber is trying to encourage the parties to avoid repetitious evidence. Have you discussed it with Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have nothing to add. We just wanted video to be admitted since it arrived late with the previous witness. It was a translator who testified on the same issue but it was late given I think to the Prosecution, so it was not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, would there be any objection against it? Then we could admit it if both parties consider it -- if the Defence considers it is relevant to present it as evidence and if you have no objections we could just look at it and have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If it's the same video we saw with Batanic a few weeks ago, then there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the same video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we don't have to play it again, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may smoothen the proceedings. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, let me first ask you something about the hospital in Blazuj. Could you just tell us briefly who worked in that hospital? Was it mobilised personnel? Was there compulsory work service? Did you hold a rank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, the hospital in Blazuj, right at the beginning, was an example of the way in which medical workers organised themselves in that area. No orders had been received, either from the military or civilian authorities, because this part of Sarajevo, which was mostly inhabited by Serbs, did not have a permanent medical care facility, and because of the attacks and other combat activities against Ilidza which was inhabited by Serbs where there were some local guards organised by the Territorial Defence, wounded were coming in, both civilians and those Territorial Defence members who were defending this area. And before the war broke out, the hospital where those people gravitated was the Kosevo Hospital and the military hospital in Sarajevo which was now the city hospital. It was very difficult to reach those two facilities at that time, and the wounded and the sick based on their experience from what happened in Dobrovoljacka Street and the fate suffered by the soldiers who were wounded and captured, they didn't want to go to the hospital. I as a doctor and a group of medical technicians, we faced this huge problems, what to do. In this situation, the local commune, which was the micro nucleus of local government, gave me catering establishment which was part of a factory Zica a metal working factory and this is where we managed to set up the first aid station, and since the injuries that we encountered as the conflict progressed required a higher level of medical care, and we were not ready to provide it, we did not have the wherewithal, we did not have the equipment, in fact we didn't even have the expertise. I was an ear, nose and throat specialist and the other two or three doctors, they were junior doctors, unexperienced doctors. So what we did, we took the civilians and the Territorial Defence members, and we sent them to the Pale hospital which was about 30 kilometres away from us. But from Blazuj or, rather, from Ilidza to Pale it took about five hours to get there because you had to take the round about route, mountain roads and so on, and so we -- unfortunately because we didn't have the equipment, many of those people died. The hospital was an example of the medical workers and the population organising themselves to provide the service. I don't know if I have answered your question, and if you're happy with my answer, but that would be it in substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic is certainly encouraged to put more focused questions to you, witness, because you've told us a lot but the relevance and probative value of it is not apparent immediately. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I would kindly ask you to look at paragraph 4 of your statement. It's at page 2 in both versions. Well, the document is already on the screen. Let us now move to page 2. Here, you talk about the 22nd of April, 1992. You talk about the attack on Ilidza. Now, relating to this paragraph of your statement, I would like to show you a document, that's 1D2827. Doctor, you see this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: It's me, and the names of the injured people were taken from the protocol of the Zica hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no English translation in e-court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll -- in this document, Your Honours, it's obvious that the translation is lacking. We just see names and on the -- beside the names usually Latin diagnoses, so I can ask shortly the doctor about the type of the wounds recorded in this document and we'll ask for the same to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could we not -- I think the Chamber has some experience, and the document apparently gives a name and then a diagnosis, and the V usually stand for wound, vulnus, and what is the right hand is clear and what is the back of the body. So I suggest that unless you want to spend considerable attention to the details of the diagnoses, that we just -- that you ask one or two questions and that we move on and wait, MFI the document, and if any surprise comes up when the English translation is produced, then we will decide on how to proceed. Ms. Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to point out that there is more than just Latin on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. So therefore I would suggest that we read at least the first line and that we also read the last three or four lines but leave it to that for the time being. Could you please read it very slowly and could you also be reminded, Mr. Lukic, that this is not the way we are usually proceeding with interpretation compared to translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Do you want me to read or would you rather the witness read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the witness could read slowly out what he reads at the heading of this document. Mr. Pejic would you please do that? Would you please read slowly aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. List of injured civilians, injured in an attack on the municipality of Ilidza on the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you now read what appears below the line which starts with number 29.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The list contains 29 entries. So a total of 29 names of injured people is on the list. The other injured and wounded persons with minor wounds, 25, were given first aid in the outpatient clinic at Ilidza. The total number of injured persons is 56 but not all of them reported at Zica but were treated elsewhere." I've already stated in the previous passage where that was. "The seriously wounded persons were brought to the hospital. In the afternoon, those people who were killed were brought to the hospital, a total of 11 people. "Signed, Dr. Milan Pejic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Lukic, I would have one question. Does your medical expertise allow you to tell them that those 29 persons were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, at that time, there was no mobilisation in force. There were no regular military forces in Ilidza. There was the Territorial Defence, and there were some village or street guards on all three sides. Based on the clothes that those people were wearing, as far as I'm concerned, they were civilians. There are documents kept regarding this incident in the protocol of the Zica hospital and -- yes, I'm sorry, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Pejic, you're answering a lot of questions which are not put to you. The real answer which I understand is, no, that your medical expertise doesn't allow you but that you gave your assessment on the basis of clothing of the people and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the rest is not asked. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is in relation to a question, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Yes, it is related to the question. I think they are civilians because I know 90 per cent of these people. They were not soldiers. They were my neighbours who live in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And none of them was affiliated with the TO or 90 per cent of the persons were totally out of the, if I could say, the armed forces or what came close to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has received quite a lot of evidence that, on both sides, all male men fit for military service were perhaps not officially recruited but at least had been armed or armed themselves in order to protect the area, et cetera, and you say it's 90 per cent, which was entirely outside the combatant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do not know that there was mobilisation then. It was only after the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska we received these papers. Now, whether there was somebody who was a policeman, no, I did not have any people in uniform. Was anybody an active soldier? No. I didn't have anyone in uniform. Did they have weapons? Perhaps hunting weapons. I don't know. I was not on the spot. It is wounded people who were brought to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn briefly to paragraph 10 of your statement. And this is what you say there. Actually we can have it on the screen again. D589. Page 3. [In English] Could we have the next page in English version too? Paragraph 10. Thank you. [Interpretation] This is what you say in this paragraph. It never mattered who were the individuals we were helping. We treated everyone equally, be them Muslims, Croats or Serbs. We helped everyone. And then you continue. This is what I'd like to ask you in this regard: To this day, are there archives in your hospital? Are their patient files?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, patient files exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me which are the ones that are accessible today and where can we find them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: If you allow me first of all I have been a doctor for very many years and I know what a medical institution should do and what kind of records should be kept. In the hospital that I headed, and where I worked, there were files on injured persons and ill persons who reported for treatment for the first time. Also there were files concerning those who were admitted for hospital treatment. There were also files on how long they were there, as in-patients and when they were sent out. Every wounded person and every ill person regardless of where they came from was given medical assistance. They were all given medical findings as well. If they were not admitted into hospital, they were given discharge papers, either from a GP stating what their condition was or discharge papers about the surgery that they had undergone and how they were treated generally. These files were kept at the Kasindol Hospital in the office where I work, and then I transferred these documents after leaving Sarajevo, Serb Sarajevo, and I issued a countless number of certificates on that basis, on woundings, and so on and so forth. Right now, they are in the headquarters of the Ilidza refugees in Sarajevo, the street of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade number 2, Prevasareska [phoen] brigada. They are accessible and all the information I presented here can be found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the last sentence was the answer to your question. It was a very long answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although I asked for the type of protocols as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question was: Could you please tell me which are the ones that are accessible today and where we can find them? That was your question. And that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking about the protocols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's in sequence to patient files exist. That's what the witness said and then you asked this question. But in general, Mr. Lukic, please keep proper control over the -- over a focused examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try my best. Maybe it will not be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, now I'd like to show you a document that is registered as 1D2033 in e-court. Dr. Pejic, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I saw it when I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document has to do with medical treatment, as we can see from the document itself, of the population and HVO combatants of the municipality of Kiseljak, 150 serious patients and so on and so forth. These 150 seriously wounded and sick individuals, would that also pertain to members of the HVO? Actually, who does it pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: It pertains to members of the HVO and the inhabitants of Herceg-Bosna. This was a report written on the 13th of October, 1993. As for the number of persons that we assisted in the years after that, that number is much bigger than this. Maybe I won't be too extensive if I say a bit more about this, if Their Honours allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say that Mr. Lukic should explain what the relevance of this is. I highly appreciate that medical services were rendered to other groups, but what's the relevance for this case? This case is not about not paying proper attention to patients. This case is about war crimes, crimes against humanity. That's what this case is about, Mr. Lukic, and what would change this, what's the relevance of this, apart from appreciation of what was done?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. This one goes to mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mens rea, mens rea of whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can continue. I had the line of questions about my client at the end, but I can proceed with that line of questions now, if you want me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then please move to that without further delay. Do you think that this has got anything to do with any instructions or was Mr. Mladic aware of all this, Mr. Pejic, to your knowledge? You sent it to civilian authorities, apparently. Although a copy was sent to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether General Mladic knew about this, that the HVO members who were involved in the Croatian-Bosnian conflict were coming to my hospital to be treated because I didn't receive any instructions. We behaved on the basis of medical ethics, the oath of Hippocrates, and the medical profession.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is speaking too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were speaking too fast. Mr. Lukic, we will invite the witness to repeat the last part of his answer, but would you then please come to your point because I'm not aware that there were charges primarily of crimes committed against HVO people, and that's what this is about, and the population of Kiseljak. Unless I misunderstood the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The term the Prosecution uses is "non-Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but in every respect only in a relevant context, Mr. Lukic. It's not everything that happened to non-Serbs the accused is blamed for. That certainly is not the gist of this indictment. As you are aware of, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is it your point that you want to say there could be no discriminatory intent because you at some points have behaved well against that members of that same ethnic group or -- is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our point is that you cannot have at one point in time and at another point in time you do not have and it goes up and down. You either have intent or you do not. I don't understand that somebody can be on the weekends only with the criminal intent and not with the same intent during the same war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I -- well, I do understand -- I notice that you do not understand that and please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejic, we see down here that this was submitted to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and, inter alia, to the Ministry of Health of Republika Srpska. Number 5 says command of the Ilidza Brigade. And number 6 is illegible. That's the document that we found. And in the English version, obviously this could not have been translated. Do you know who is referred to under number 6? Can you see it from the document? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The command of the Igman Brigade, because we were duty-bound to do that as well. So this is the command of the Igman Brigade. It was these two brigades that were in this area, namely this was their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the addressees that this document was sent to, number 1, Main Staff of the VRS; number 5, the command of the Ilidza Brigade; number 6, command of the Igman Brigade, did you ever receive orders from any of them or instructions or recommendations to the effect that Muslims and Croats should not be treated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Ratko Mladic ever visit your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On those occasions, did he talk to the patients, the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He visited all the wounded, and all the patients, the ill people, and he talked to me as head of the hospital. And irrespective of ethnicity, he shook hands with practically all the patients, all the wounded persons and ill persons. As far as I remember he was very cordially greeted by all. This happened 20 years ago so I cannot remember each and every moment but never was there a single word from General Mladic to the effect that somebody should not be treated at this hospital and that someone did not belong to that hospital at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I didn't object to that question but none of Mr. Mladic's appearances at the hospital, what he did or what he said, was provided in the statement so we have no notice of General Mladic's presence there. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just for the next time we should receive such notice, particularly about the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the next time but this, we have had quite many next times in this respect. Mr. Lukic, anywhere in the statement where you discuss the presence or Mr. Mladic visiting the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just ask my colleague Mr. Ivetic if he can find it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should be on top of the statement in such a way when examining the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I saw it but obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's move on, and then -- there is another matter I'm looking at the clock. We could proceed in two ways. We could take a 20-minutes break and then continue for another quarter of an hour or we could skip one of the breaks because we had a very long first session and then, for example, finish at -- in 15 or 20 minutes from now, which would be a session of one hour but then to finish for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's better to continue, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no, I do not at all. So therefore we will skip the next break and we will continue until ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour, now? Thank you. We to tender this document into evidence. I would cut then my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2033 receives number D590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D590 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to have on our screens 1D3086.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, when did we receive this document from you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was yesterday, but I do think, yes, I gave it to you yesterday during our proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because we don't have the translation of this document, so I will very briefly ask you if you could read the title of this document for us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: "Injured civilians treated in the Zica hospital in the course of 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "civilians," what did you mean by that? Who was covered by this term?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: When I say civilians, I mean all those people who were not part of the Republika Srpska army, women, men, children, Croats, Croats who were not soldiers in the Republika Srpska army, because here you have a significant number of Croats who are on this list. Some were soldiers and some were not, and we treated them as HVO members, and as far as we were concerned, they were civilians. Furthermore, these were people who did not live in the area of responsibility of the Republika Srpska army. They lived in a different region, in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But how did they come to be in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: They were brought there in various transportation -- means of transportation, in ambulances, in motor vehicles, and in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who brought them there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Croats were bringing them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As regards this list, do you know how many HVO members are listed here, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say, but I think that there are 130 or so Croats on this list. All of them were listed as HVO. I don't know whether they were in the actual fact members of the HVO or not. And in light of the fact that the -- you had military and civilian authorities in that region, just as you had in our region, we treated them as civilians because they were not residents of the Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, having now listened to a long story about Croats, possibly including HVO members being treated in that hospital, is there any dispute about it? I mean, you don't have to agree on it but if there is no dispute about it, for whatever reason, because you do not consider it relevant or -- then tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: For one thing it's not very clear where this list comes from. So while the witness says it's covers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's assume that it's a truthful list, would that change your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I would generally object to the admission of this document because I don't see the relevance of it but I cannot verify or not whether -- I don't have an objection to that there is Croats on this list, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you have no objections or at least you do not challenge that Croats and including HVO members have been treated at that hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even without seeing that list?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it seems to be a rather useless exercise what we are doing at this moment. Please proceed. There is no dispute. Only thing is that a list --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just heard that there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you could have asked before. You're under a constant duty to wonder whether what you present as evidence is on an issue which is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a little clarification for myself. Doctor, are you saying at page 78 lines 14 to 20, you say all of them were listed as HVO. I don't know whether they were in the actual fact members of the HVO or not, and in light of the fact that you had military and civilian authorities in the region, just as you had in our region, we treated them as civilians. Now, if you didn't know that they were HVO, why did you list them as HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I listed them as HVO because of the area where they lived. The area where they lived was under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then you go on to say but you treated them as civilians. Are they HVO or are they civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a question that you should ask of the people from the area. What's the formation they belong to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I asked you because you just told us this, just a second. I'm quoting what you said. You said: And in light of the fact that they, and you had military and civilian authorities in that region just as you had in our region, we treated them as civilians. So you treated them as civilians but you say they are HVO. I'm not following your story.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as we were concerned, we didn't care if our patients were military or civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. That's not my question. My question is why do you call them HVO, or call them civilians, and why do you list them as HVO if you don't know that they are HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we did not consider them to be members of the Republika Srpska army and yet they came from an area that was controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you call them HVO and then you treat them as civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We called them HVO but we treated them as patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said civilians, not patients.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for us doctors, doing our job, it's all the same. We don't care if they are civilians or soldiers, I cannot treat civilians and soldiers differently. I mean, medically treat. We had the same approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One follow-up. We have Mr. Pejic, we have this list on the screen. When was this list compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This list was done in 1994, I think. We were duty-bound to report, yes, the Ministry of Health and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have answered my question. We see 24 entries. You said earlier that there were 150 on the list. Are there more pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Definitely, I think so. There are no HVO members on this particular list here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My question is answered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I just want to inform Your Honours this document has 19 pages, the first 17 pages is about the wounded person and two last pages about killed persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, let me go back first to the question asked by His Honour Judge Moloto. Were there cases when Croats in military uniforms were brought in, either injured or sick?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: They were brought in by persons wearing military uniforms, not exclusively soldiers but sometimes a -- medical technicians, civilians, would bring them there. Those who worked in the hospital that had been established in Kiseljak but as far as I can remember, no wounded Croatian Defence Council soldiers were brought in in uniform. They were all given medical treatment and because the medical staff in the Kiseljak hospital could not treat them, they would send them on to us but they were in civilian clothes or, rather, they wore the usual hospital gowns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who made this list and what is it based on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: The specialist service in the hospital made this list and I signed it. It was based on the protocols, the files that I was talking about at the beginning of this hearing. And this list is available. You can verify it against the protocols at any moment, if the Prosecution wants to do it, they are free to do it of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have page 1 of this document in front of us, and I would like you to look at number 6. What is the ethnicity of this person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: It's Almir Cutina. He is a Muslim or a Bosniak, as we call them now, and at that time he was 17. Well, number 7 again but you didn't ask me about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, despite the questions put by the Judges which are about consistency in the use of words, there was no dispute about other ethnicities being treated. We then talked about Croats and HVO. But I took it, Ms. Hasan, that you are not claiming that any distinction was made for young Muslim boys or that they would be treated as well at least that you would not dispute if that is the evidence. Now we go again in great detail about the same issue, Mr. Lukic. Let's talk about what is primarily charged and that is not that 16-year-old Muslim boys were not treated in Blazuj. And there is no dispute about the matter. So please consider that carefully. I said we would stop at ten minutes to 2.00, we are close to that point in time. Reconsider your line of questioning, Mr. Lukic, apart from the limited time that is left, if I understood your assessment well. Mr. Pejic, we will adjourn for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom and I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way to whomever about your testimony, either given or still to be given. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two issues I would briefly want to address. First, the list which is without translation, that's 1D2827. I think it should be marked for identification pending a translation. You almost need a translation from Latin into English. But, Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2827 receives number D591, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Then the video MFI'd as D523, I suggested to you, Mr. Lukic, that it would not have to be played. I looked a bit in the history of D523. The Chamber has seen it. So that would not be a reason to play it again. At the same time, of course, you announced at the time when Mr. Batanic testified that it would be identified by Dr. Pejic as -- because you were -- the Prosecution was asking about the source of it. Therefore, I would -- I don't know how long it is exactly, it's relatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's relatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just under two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just under two minutes. Then I suggest that it can be played but without translation, we don't have to play it twice because the main purpose is to seek confirmation by Dr. Pejic of what was the claim, that it's him and that what he said there is in accordance with the truth and we all have the transcripts. We adjourn for the day and we resume --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- sorry to interrupt you but Your Honours asked me to report back on the e-mails related to Mr. Nikolic. We have no further follow-up and from our perspective there is no need for further restrictions on his communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please pass on the message to the Victims and Witness Section that witness Nikolic is free to communicate with whomever he wants, including the testimony he has given. We adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 23rd of July at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of July, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.
